name: Greater Yang Accumulation of Water
description: Greater Yang Accumulation of Water (Tài Yáng Xù Shuǐ Zhèng, 太阳蓄水证) is a full TCM pattern affecting the Bladder. Key signs: Difficult or scanty urination, Int...

timing_worsening_explanation: Symptoms often develop several days into a common cold or flu that was either untreated or treated incorrectly (particularly if sweating therapy was used too aggressively). The thirst and urinary difficulty tend to worsen through the day as fluid intake accumulates without being properly processed. Symptoms may be worse in damp or cold weather. The pattern can develop relatively quickly (over a few days) from a straightforward exterior cold invasion if circumstances allow the pathogen to enter deeper.
practitioner_notes:
The diagnostic logic of Greater Yang Accumulation of Water centres on a key triad: difficulty urinating, intense thirst, and mild fever with a floating pulse. The reasoning runs as follows: an initial exterior Cold attack (the Greater Yang stage) was either untreated or treated incorrectly. Rather than being expelled through sweating, the pathogenic influence travelled inward along the Bladder channel and disrupted the Bladder's ability to transform and move fluids. This is sometimes described as the pathogen entering the 'fu organ' (hollow organ) aspect of the Greater Yang rather than remaining at the surface.
The central paradox of this pattern is instructive: the person is extremely thirsty yet cannot properly use the water they drink. Body fluids are pooling in the lower abdomen because the Bladder's Qi transformation is impaired. Since fluids cannot be properly distributed upward, the mouth and throat feel parched. Yet because fluids cannot move downward into urine either, the lower abdomen feels full and distended. In severe cases, water drunk immediately comes back up as vomiting, which the Shang Han Lun specifically names shui ni (water counterflow). The floating pulse and mild fever tell the practitioner that the original exterior condition has not yet fully resolved, making this a combined exterior-interior pattern with the interior water accumulation as the primary problem.
The key differentiating question is whether the person's urine output is reduced. If someone has lower abdominal distension with mental agitation but urinates normally, the pattern is more likely Greater Yang Blood Accumulation rather than Water Accumulation. This distinction, highlighted in classical texts, relies on checking whether "urination is normal" (pointing to Blood Accumulation) versus "urination is difficult" (pointing to Water Accumulation).
pathophysiology: An unresolved exterior Cold pathogen penetrates inward to the Bladder, disrupting its ability to transform and excrete fluids, so water accumulates in the lower abdomen while the rest of the body paradoxically lacks moisture.
treatment_principle: Warm Yang and promote Qi transformation, drain water accumulation and resolve the exterior
typical_timeline: 3-10 days for acute presentations when treated with herbs and/or acupuncture. Most cases resolve within one week with appropriate Wu Ling San treatment.
formula_modifications:
If the person is vomiting water immediately after drinking (Water Rebellion / Shui Ni): This indicates a more severe form of the pattern where accumulated water pushes upward into the Stomach. The standard Wu Ling San is still used but should be taken in smaller, more frequent doses with warm water to avoid triggering further vomiting. Some practitioners add Ban Xia (Pinellia) to help settle the Stomach and direct rebellious Qi downward.
If there is noticeable swelling or puffiness (oedema): Add Fu Ping (Duckweed) or Yi Yi Ren (Coix Seed) to strengthen the water-draining effect and address fluid overflow into the tissues.
If the person still has noticeable chills, body aches, and other exterior cold symptoms: Increase the dose of Gui Zhi or add a small amount of Ma Huang to strengthen the exterior-releasing action and help open the skin pores, which in turn aids the downward movement of fluids.
If the person feels very fatigued with poor appetite and loose stools: This suggests the Spleen is significantly weakened. Increase the dose of Bai Zhu and Fu Ling, and consider adding Dang Shen (Codonopsis) or Huang Qi (Astragalus) to bolster Spleen Qi and support the body's fluid-processing capacity.
If there are signs of developing heat (yellow urine, slight irritability, yellow tongue coating): Reduce or remove Gui Zhi and add Hua Shi (Talcum) and Mu Tong (Akebia Caulis) to clear heat from the Lower Jiao while still promoting urination. This modification moves the formula closer to the approach of Zhu Ling Tang.

causes_details:
[{"cause_title": "Wind-Cold invading the exterior and transmitting inward to the Bladder", "explanation": "This is the classical and most common cause. It begins when Wind-Cold attacks the body's surface (the Greater Yang / Tai Yang layer), producing the familiar symptoms of a cold: chills, fever, headache, and body aches. In some people, the exterior pathogen is not fully expelled. After about six or seven days, the pathogenic influence follows the Bladder channel inward from the surface to the Bladder organ itself.
The Bladder's main job in TCM is to store and transform fluids, a process driven by Qi transformation (the body's ability to process and move water). When the pathogen disrupts this function, the Bladder can no longer properly separate clean fluids from waste. Water accumulates in the Lower Jiao instead of being excreted as urine, leading to the hallmark combination of reduced urination, lower abdominal fullness, and paradoxical thirst (the body has plenty of water but cannot distribute it upward to moisten the mouth)."}, {"cause_title": "Improper sweating treatment damaging Yang Qi", "explanation": "In the Shang Han Lun framework, this pattern often arises as a consequence of incorrect treatment. When a Greater Yang exterior pattern is treated with excessive sweating (too strong a dose of diaphoretic herbs, or sweating for too long), two things can happen: the exterior pathogen may not be fully expelled, and the body's Yang Qi is weakened by the excessive fluid loss.
Yang Qi is what powers the Bladder's fluid-processing function. When it is damaged by over-sweating, the Bladder loses its ability to transform and excrete water. Fluids begin to accumulate rather than circulate. The person develops thirst (because fluids cannot rise to moisten the upper body), scanty urination (because fluids cannot be pushed downward and out), and may still have low-grade fever and a floating pulse (because the original exterior pathogen lingers). This is the scenario described in Shang Han Lun line 71."}, {"cause_title": "Excessive water intake during illness", "explanation": "During an acute illness, a person may drink large amounts of water thinking it will help recovery. However, if the body's fluid-processing capacity is already compromised by the illness, drinking too much water overwhelms the system. The Spleen and Bladder cannot transform and transport all the incoming fluid, so it pools in the lower abdomen or rises up to the Stomach.
In severe cases, this creates what the Shang Han Lun calls 'Water Rebellion' (Shui Ni): the person is thirsty and drinks, but the water immediately comes back up as vomiting, because the Stomach is already full of unprocessed fluid that has nowhere to go. Despite vomiting, the thirst persists because the problem is not a lack of fluid in the body but an inability to distribute it properly."}]

formulas.name: Wu Ling San
formulas.description: The primary and representative formula for this pattern. Wu Ling San (Five-Ingredient Powder with Poria) consists of Ze Xie, Fu Ling, Zhu Ling, Bai Zhu, and Gui Zhi. It promotes urination, warms Yang, and restores Qi transformation in the Bladder while releasing any remaining exterior pathogen. This is the formula Zhang Zhongjing specifically created for Greater Yang Accumulation of Water.

formulas.name: Ling Gui Zhu Gan Tang
formulas.description: Used when the pattern has evolved beyond the acute exterior-interior presentation into a more chronic state of Yang deficiency with water-Dampness retention in the middle Jiao. Characterized by dizziness, palpitations below the heart, and a sensation of fullness in the chest, without the marked thirst seen in the classic Water Accumulation pattern.

herbs.name: Ze Xie
herbs.description: The chief herb in Wu Ling San. Ze Xie (Water Plantain Rhizome) strongly promotes urination, drains accumulated water from the Bladder, and clears Dampness from the Lower Jiao.

herbs.name: Fu Ling
herbs.description: Promotes urination and leaches out Dampness while also strengthening the Spleen. Supports the Spleen's role in transforming and transporting fluids so they circulate properly rather than pooling.

herbs.name: Zhu Ling
herbs.description: A powerful water-draining herb that works alongside Fu Ling and Ze Xie. Zhu Ling specifically promotes urination and eliminates Dampness, helping restore the downward flow of fluids through the Bladder.

herbs.name: Gui Zhi
herbs.description: Warms Yang and promotes Qi transformation in the Bladder while also gently releasing any remaining exterior pathogen. Gui Zhi acts like kindling under a cauldron, providing the warmth needed for the Bladder to resume its fluid-processing function.

herbs.name: Bai Zhu
herbs.description: Strengthens the Spleen and dries Dampness. By supporting the Spleen's transforming and transporting function, Bai Zhu helps ensure fluids are properly distributed throughout the body rather than accumulating.

acupoints.name: Zhongji REN-3
acupoints.description: The Front-Mu (alarm) point of the Bladder. Directly activates Bladder Qi transformation and promotes urination to drain accumulated water from the Lower Jiao.

acupoints.name: Pangguangshu BL-28
acupoints.description: The Back-Shu (transporting) point of the Bladder. Paired with Zhongji REN-3 as a classic Front-Mu/Back-Shu combination to powerfully restore Bladder Qi transformation and resolve water accumulation.

acupoints.name: Sanyinjiao SP-6
acupoints.description: Meeting point of the three Yin channels of the leg. Strengthens the Spleen's fluid-transporting function and supports urination. Helps address the underlying Spleen weakness that allows water to accumulate.

acupoints.name: Yinlingquan SP-9
acupoints.description: The He-Sea point of the Spleen channel, specifically indicated for resolving Dampness and promoting urination. One of the most important points for draining water and Dampness from the Lower Jiao.

acupoints.name: Weiyang BL-39
acupoints.description: The Lower He-Sea point of the San Jiao (Triple Burner). Regulates the waterways of the San Jiao and promotes fluid metabolism throughout all three Jiao, directly addressing the Qi transformation failure at the root of this pattern.

acupoints.name: Zusanli ST-36
acupoints.description: Strengthens the Spleen and Stomach to support proper fluid transformation and transportation. Bolsters overall Qi to help the body process and distribute fluids correctly.

faqs.question: What is Greater Yang Accumulation of Water in TCM?
faqs.answer: An unresolved exterior Cold pathogen penetrates inward to the Bladder, disrupting its ability to transform and excrete fluids, so water accumulates in the lower abdomen while the rest of the body paradoxically lacks moisture.

faqs.question: What are the key signs of Greater Yang Accumulation of Water?
faqs.answer: Key signs include: Difficult or scanty urination, Intense thirst with desire to drink, Lower abdominal fullness and distension, Mild fever, Slight aversion to wind or cold, Headache, Vomiting of water immediately after drinking, Restlessness or irritability, A sense of heaviness in the lower abdomen, Nausea.

faqs.question: What formulas treat Greater Yang Accumulation of Water?
faqs.answer: Common formulas for Greater Yang Accumulation of Water include: Wu Ling San, Ling Gui Zhu Gan Tang.

faqs.question: What Western conditions relate to Greater Yang Accumulation of Water?
faqs.answer: This pattern is associated with: Acute urinary retention, Oedema, Acute gastroenteritis with vomiting, Nephrotic syndrome, Neurogenic bladder dysfunction, Post-febrile fluid retention.

faqs.question: What is the treatment principle for Greater Yang Accumulation of Water?
faqs.answer: Warm Yang and promote Qi transformation, drain water accumulation and resolve the exterior
